category: Core vocabulary: work and the office

entries.meaning: The place where a person does their job. ---
examples: Cell phones aren't allowed in the workplace.
The company is trying to make the workplace safer.
These rules apply in most American workplaces.

entries.meaning: A small work area separated from the rest of an office by low walls. ---
examples: He spends nine hours a day in a cubicle.
Somebody taped a birthday sign to her cubicle.
They tore out the cubicles and went open-plan.

entries.meaning: The counter near the entrance where visitors check in. ---
examples: Leave your name at the front desk.
The front desk called up to say my ride was here.
Both front desks were empty at that hour.

entries.meaning: Someone whose job is to greet visitors and answer the phone at an office. ---
examples: The receptionist buzzed us in.
Ask the receptionist for a visitor badge.
They hired two more receptionists for the clinic.

entries.meaning: A place at a workplace or school where meals are served and eaten. ---
examples: We had lunch in the company cafeteria.
The cafeteria closes at two.
Both cafeterias serve the same sandwiches.

entries.meaning: A room at work where employees can eat, rest, or make coffee. ---
examples: There's leftover pizza in the break room.
Somebody left a mess in the break room again.
The break rooms on both floors have microwaves.

entries.meaning: One of the sections a company or organization is divided into. ---
examples: She works in the accounting department.
That's a question for the legal department.
Three departments share the same floor.

entries.meaning: A group of people working together for a shared purpose. ---
examples: She runs a nonprofit organization.
The whole organization got the same email.
Several organizations signed the letter.
entries.contrast: Americans spell it with a z; the British usually write organisation.

entries.meaning: A machine that puts text or images from a computer onto paper. ---
examples: The printer is out of paper again.
Send it to the printer on the third floor.
Both printers are jammed.

entries.meaning: A machine that makes paper copies of documents. ---
examples: The copier jams every other day.
She stood at the copier for twenty minutes.
They finally replaced both copiers.
entries.contrast: Also called a photocopier; Americans often just say the copy machine.

entries.meaning: A small bent piece of wire that holds sheets of paper together. ---
examples: Hand me a paperclip.
The whole packet was held together with one paperclip.
There's a box of paperclips in the drawer.
entries.contrast: Often written as two words: paper clip.

entries.meaning: A stiff folder with rings inside that hold punched pages. ---
examples: Everything for the class is in this binder.
She put the contract in a three-ring binder.
The binders are on the shelf by the window.

entries.meaning: A folded cover for holding loose papers, or a place for files on a computer. ---
examples: Put the receipts in a folder.
I saved it in a folder on my desktop.
There were a dozen folders stacked on his chair.

entries.meaning: A smooth white panel you write on with markers that wipe off. ---
examples: She drew the whole plan on the whiteboard.
Somebody erased the whiteboard before we finished.
Every conference room has a whiteboard.

entries.meaning: A device that shines an image from a computer onto a screen or wall. ---
examples: The projector won't connect to my laptop.
Dim the lights and turn on the projector.
Both projectors are booked for that hour.

entries.meaning: The screen you look at when using a computer. ---
examples: He works with two monitors.
The monitor keeps flickering.
IT ordered a bigger monitor for her desk.

entries.meaning: The set of keys you type on to control a computer. ---
examples: I spilled coffee on my keyboard.
This keyboard is way too loud.
They ordered new keyboards for the whole floor.

entries.meaning: A small portable computer that folds shut. ---
examples: Bring your laptop to the meeting.
My laptop died halfway through the call.
The company issues laptops to everyone.

entries.meaning: An electronic machine for storing information and doing work with it. ---
examples: My computer is running really slow today.
Turn the computer off before you leave.
All the computers were updated overnight.

entries.meaning: A book of blank pages for writing notes in. ---
examples: She takes notes in a little notebook.
I left my notebook in the conference room.
There's a stack of notebooks in the supply closet.

entries.meaning: A writing instrument that uses ink. ---
examples: Do you have a pen I can borrow?
The pen ran out halfway through the form.
Somebody keeps walking off with my pens.

entries.meaning: A writing instrument with a thin stick of graphite inside. ---
examples: Fill out the form in pen, not pencil.
He sat there chewing on a pencil.
These pencils all need sharpening.

entries.meaning: A small piece of rubber or felt used to rub out writing. ---
examples: Is there an eraser on that pencil?
She rubbed the line out with an eraser.
The erasers for the whiteboard have disappeared again.
entries.contrast: American word; the British say rubber for the pencil kind.

entries.meaning: A flat paper cover that a letter goes into for mailing. ---
examples: He sealed the check in an envelope.
Write the address on the envelope.
There's a box of envelopes by the printer.

entries.meaning: A chart or program showing the days of the year and what is planned on them. ---
examples: Put it on the calendar so I don't forget.
My calendar is packed all week.
Our calendars never seem to line up.
entries.contrast: Ends in -ar, not -er, even though it sounds like -er.

entries.meaning: Paper, envelopes, and other writing supplies. ---
examples: The office orders all its stationery online.
We're out of stationery again.
She keeps the stationery in the bottom drawer.
entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like stationary ('not moving'); the paper one ends in -ery.

entries.meaning: The everyday materials a workplace uses up, like paper and pens. ---
examples: We're low on office supplies.
The supplies are kept in the closet by the copier.
Order more supplies before the end of the month.
entries.contrast: Used in the plural for office materials — a supply means something else.

entries.meaning: A small square of paper with glue on one edge, used for short reminders. ---
examples: He left a sticky note on my monitor.
The whole report was covered in sticky notes.
Write it on a sticky note so you remember.

entries.meaning: A written account of work done or facts found out. ---
examples: The report is due Friday morning.
She wrote a twelve-page report on the numbers.
Nobody reads these reports anyway.

entries.meaning: A talk in which someone shows and explains information to a group. ---
examples: I'm giving a presentation to the whole department.
His presentation ran about ten minutes long.
We sat through four presentations in a row.

entries.meaning: A computer document laid out in rows and columns for numbers. ---
examples: Everything's tracked in one big spreadsheet.
She sent me the spreadsheet with the budget in it.
He keeps three separate spreadsheets for expenses.

entries.meaning: A piece of writing that gives official information or a record. ---
examples: Sign the document at the bottom of page two.
I can't open the document you sent.
Bring both documents to the meeting.

entries.meaning: An arrangement that two sides have accepted. ---
examples: We finally reached an agreement.
The agreement covers the next three years.
Both agreements were signed the same day.

entries.meaning: The list of a company's employees and the money paid to them. ---
examples: There are forty people on the payroll.
Talk to payroll about the missing hours.
Both payrolls are handled by the same office.

entries.meaning: The forms and written records a job requires. ---
examples: There's a mountain of paperwork on his desk.
I spent all morning on paperwork.
You can't start until the paperwork goes through.
entries.contrast: Uncountable — say a lot of paperwork, never paperworks.

entries.meaning: A printed sheet with blank spaces to be filled in. ---
examples: Fill out this form and bring it back.
The form asks for your Social Security number.
There were four forms to sign on my first day.

entries.meaning: A set of questions asked of many people to collect opinions. ---
examples: HR sent out an employee survey.
The survey takes about five minutes.
Nobody fills out these surveys.
entries.contrast: Stress moves: the noun is SUR-vay, the verb to survey is sur-VAY.

entries.meaning: A ready-made pattern you fill in to make a document. ---
examples: Just use the template instead of starting over.
The template already has the logo on it.
There are templates for all the standard letters.

entries.meaning: Your name written by hand to show you agree to something. ---
examples: We just need your signature here.
The signature on the check didn't match.
They collected signatures from everyone on the team.
entries.contrast: The g is pronounced here, though it is silent in sign.

entries.meaning: A short written summary of your work history, sent when applying for a job. ---
examples: Send me your resume and I'll pass it along.
Her resume is two pages long.
They got over two hundred resumes for one opening.
entries.contrast: Often written résumé. The noun is REZ-uh-may; the verb resume ('start again') is rih-ZOOM.

entries.meaning: A letter sent with a resume explaining why you want the job. ---
examples: Don't send a resume without a cover letter.
Her cover letter was better than the resume.
He rewrites the cover letter for every job.

entries.meaning: A written plan or offer put forward for others to consider. ---
examples: We're putting together a proposal for the client.
The proposal got turned down.
They reviewed six proposals before choosing one.

entries.meaning: The written record of what was said and decided at a meeting. ---
examples: Who's taking the minutes today?
The minutes from last week are attached.
She reads the minutes out loud at the start.
entries.contrast: Always plural in this meaning — never a minute of a meeting.

entries.meaning: An occasion when people come together to discuss work. ---
examples: I've got a meeting at ten.
That meeting could have been an email.
His calendar is nothing but back-to-back meetings.

entries.meaning: A large organized event where people meet to hear talks about their field. ---
examples: She's speaking at a conference in Denver.
The conference runs Tuesday through Thursday.
He goes to two or three conferences a year.

entries.meaning: A conversation by phone or video, especially a work one. ---
examples: I'm on a call until eleven.
Let's set up a call for Monday.
She had five calls back to back.

entries.meaning: The time by which something has to be finished. ---
examples: The deadline is end of day Friday.
We missed the deadline by two hours.
He works better with tight deadlines.

entries.meaning: A plan showing when things will happen. ---
examples: My schedule is full this week.
The project is behind schedule.
They post the schedules every Sunday night.
entries.contrast: Americans say SKEJ-ool; the British say SHED-yool.

entries.meaning: Something you are trying to achieve. ---
examples: Our goal is to double sales this year.
She set a goal of finishing by June.
We hit all three goals for the quarter.

entries.meaning: The latest news about how something is going. ---
examples: Can you give me a quick update?
There's been no update since Tuesday.
He sends updates every Friday afternoon.
entries.contrast: Stress moves: the noun is UP-dayt, the verb to update is up-DAYT.

entries.meaning: A careful look at how well someone or something is doing. ---
examples: I have my performance review next week.
The review went better than I expected.
They do reviews twice a year here.

entries.meaning: The paid position a person holds. ---
examples: He got a job at a bank downtown.
She's been at the same job for eleven years.
He worked two jobs to pay for school.
entries.contrast: Countable, unlike work: say two jobs, never two works.

entries.meaning: A particular job within an organization. ---
examples: I'm applying for a position in marketing.
The position has been open since March.
They're filling three positions this fall.

entries.meaning: The job or function a person has on a team. ---
examples: She just moved into a management role.
My role is mostly writing and editing.
The two roles overlap quite a bit.

entries.meaning: A kind of work that requires training and a formal qualification. ---
examples: Teaching is a demanding profession.
He left the legal profession at forty.
Nursing and law are very different professions.

entries.meaning: A move to a more senior job in the same organization. ---
examples: She got a promotion after two years.
The promotion came with a bigger office.
They announced three promotions at once.

entries.meaning: The act of formally quitting a job, or the letter announcing it. ---
examples: He handed in his resignation on Monday.
Her resignation took everyone by surprise.
Two resignations landed in the same week.
entries.contrast: The g is pronounced here, though it is silent in resign.

entries.meaning: The health insurance, paid leave, and other extras an employer provides. ---
examples: The pay is average but the benefits are great.
Part-timers don't get benefits.
Benefits kick in after ninety days.
entries.contrast: Plural in this sense — a benefit on its own just means an advantage.

entries.meaning: Time off work for rest or travel. ---
examples: I'm taking a vacation in August.
She's on vacation until the tenth.
We get three weeks of vacation a year.
entries.contrast: American; the British say holiday for the same thing.

entries.meaning: Officially approved time away from work. ---
examples: She's on maternity leave until March.
He took two weeks of unpaid leave.
You have to request leave a month ahead.
entries.contrast: Uncountable in this sense — never leaves for time off work.

entries.meaning: Hours worked beyond the normal schedule, or the extra pay for them. ---
examples: He's been working a lot of overtime.
Overtime pays time and a half.
There's no overtime in the budget this month.

entries.meaning: A set period of working hours, one of several covering the day. ---
examples: My shift starts at six in the morning.
She picked up an extra shift on Saturday.
The night shifts are hardest to fill.

entries.meaning: The regular trip between home and work. ---
examples: My commute is about forty minutes each way.
He reads on the commute into the city.
Long commutes wear people down.

entries.meaning: The person who directs and checks another employee's work. ---
examples: Ask your supervisor before you leave early.
My supervisor signed off on the request.
Both supervisors were in the meeting.

entries.meaning: Someone you work with. ---
examples: A coworker gave me a ride home.
She's friendly with everyone, but her coworkers barely know her.
Two coworkers covered my shift.
entries.contrast: Also written co-worker.

entries.meaning: A student or trainee doing short-term work to gain experience. ---
examples: The intern handles the scheduling.
She started here as an intern.
We take on four interns every summer.
entries.contrast: Stress moves: the noun is IN-turn, the verb to intern is in-TURN.

entries.meaning: A person being considered for a job. ---
examples: He's the strongest candidate we've seen.
The candidate asked good questions.
They narrowed it down to three candidates.

entries.meaning: A formal written request for a job or a place somewhere. ---
examples: I sent in my application last night.
The application takes about half an hour.
They got six hundred applications for one job.

entries.meaning: A meeting where an employer questions someone applying for a job. ---
examples: I have an interview Thursday afternoon.
The interview lasted almost two hours.
She went through four interviews before the offer.

entries.meaning: A formal proposal to hire someone at a stated salary. ---
examples: She got an offer from a firm in Boston.
The offer came in below what he wanted.
He turned down two offers last month.

entries.meaning: Teaching that prepares someone to do a job. ---
examples: New hires get two weeks of training.
She's still in training.
The training was mostly videos.
entries.contrast: Uncountable — say a lot of training, not trainings.

entries.meaning: An organized group of workers formed to protect their rights. ---
examples: The union is negotiating a new contract.
He's been in the union since 1998.
Two unions represent workers at the plant.

entries.meaning: A refusal to work, used to press an employer for something. ---
examples: The drivers went on strike for two weeks.
The strike ended with a wage increase.
There were strikes at three plants that summer.

entries.meaning: The dismissal of workers because there is not enough work or money. ---
examples: He lost his job in the last layoff.
The layoff hit the whole department.
There were layoffs right before the holidays.

entries.meaning: The amount of work a person is expected to do. ---
examples: My workload has doubled since she left.
They finally cut back his workload.
Workloads are uneven across the team.

entries.meaning: Exhaustion caused by working too hard for too long. ---
examples: Burnout is why she quit.
There's a lot of burnout in that field.
He's showing every sign of burnout.

entries.meaning: The general mood and confidence of a group of people. ---
examples: Morale is pretty low right now.
The bonuses did nothing for morale.
New management brought morale back up.
entries.contrast: Stress falls on the second syllable, muh-RAL — not the same word as moral.

entries.meaning: The people employed by an organization. ---
examples: All personnel have to badge in.
Personnel were evacuated within minutes.
Ask personnel about your benefits.
entries.contrast: Stress falls on the last syllable, pur-suh-NEL — don't confuse it with personal.

entries.meaning: Someone employed to clean and maintain a building. ---
examples: The janitor let us into the room.
He worked as a janitor while going to school.
The janitors come through around eight.
entries.contrast: American; the British say caretaker.

entries.meaning: Someone who works for several clients instead of one employer. ---
examples: She's been a freelancer since 2019.
We brought in a freelancer to finish the design.
Most of our writers are freelancers.

entries.meaning: A person or company hired to do a job without being an employee. ---
examples: He works there as a contractor, not staff.
The contractor bills by the hour.
Half the team are contractors.

entries.meaning: A planned piece of work with a goal and an end date. ---
examples: I'm on a new project starting Monday.
The project is running two weeks late.
She's juggling three projects at once.
entries.contrast: Stress moves: the noun is PRAH-jekt, the verb to project is pruh-JEKT.

entries.meaning: A single piece of work that has to be done. ---
examples: That's the first task on my list.
It's a boring task, but somebody has to do it.
He knocked out three tasks before lunch.

entries.meaning: A job or duty given to someone. ---
examples: She got the overseas assignment.
This assignment should take a couple of days.
He turns down assignments he doesn't like.

entries.meaning: Something you are required to do as part of a job. ---
examples: Answering the phone isn't part of my duty.
Her duties include scheduling and payroll.
He listed all the duties in the job posting.

entries.meaning: A set of steps followed to get something done. ---
examples: The hiring process takes about a month.
We're changing the whole process next quarter.
Both processes end up in the same place.
entries.contrast: Americans say PRAH-sess; the British say PROH-sess.

entries.meaning: How well someone does their work, or a single show put on for an audience. ---
examples: Her performance this year has been excellent.
We talk about performance in the annual review.
The company's performance slipped in the fall.
entries.countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings

entries.meaning: A formal statement that something is wrong or unfair. ---
examples: A customer filed a complaint about the delay.
The complaint went straight to HR.
They've had three complaints about the same guy.

entries.meaning: A message sent electronically, or the system for sending such messages. ---
examples: I'll send you an email this afternoon.
Just let me know by email.
There were ninety unread emails after vacation.
entries.countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings

entries.meaning: The place where incoming email messages arrive. ---
examples: My inbox is out of control.
It's sitting in your inbox somewhere.
She keeps two separate inboxes.

entries.meaning: A file sent along with an email. ---
examples: You forgot the attachment again.
The attachment is too big to send.
Don't open attachments from people you don't know.

entries.meaning: The people who run a company, or the work of running it. ---
examples: Management decided to close the store.
She moved into management last year.
There's no trust between staff and management.

entries.meaning: The work of promoting and selling a company's products. ---
examples: She works in marketing.
They spent a fortune on marketing.
The whole marketing team is remote.

entries.meaning: The part of a business that sells, or the amount of goods sold. ---
examples: Sales were down last quarter.
He's been in sales his whole career.
The sales team hit its target.
entries.contrast: Plural in this sense, with a plural verb: sales are up.

entries.meaning: People working together effectively toward a shared goal. ---
examples: That project took real teamwork.
There's not much teamwork on that floor.
The whole training is about teamwork.

entries.meaning: Deep knowledge or skill in a particular area.
examples: We hired her for her expertise in tax law.
That's outside my expertise.
The team lacks expertise in this area.
entries.contrast: Uncountable — never expertises.
